item.title: CM Afridi slams Governor Kundi for 'unconstitutional' meetings, claims move intended to provoke KP govt
item.description:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday slammed Governor Faisal Karim Kundi for holding “unconstitutional” meetings, contending that the move was an “attack on democracy”.

His remarks came a day after Governor Kundi chaired a meeting with the KP chief secretary and inspector general (IG) on the province’s security situation.

Addressing the 60th cabinet meeting in Peshawar, Afridi said that the KP governor, who belonged to the PPP, staged a “drama” yesterday by summoning the meeting and termed the move “unconstitutional”.

“The governor convening such a meeting in the presence of a provincial government with a two-thirds majority is unacceptable,” he said.

“The provincial assembly, cabinet and government are fully functional and intact,” the PTI leader asserted, terming Kundi’s act an “attack on the Constitution and democracy”.

Afridi contended that the purpose of the governor’s “unconstitutional activities” was to “provoke the provincial government and force it to react”.

However, he advised PTI workers to stay peaceful and abide by the law and the Constitution.

Calling on the province’s chief secretary and IG, the chief minister urged them not to comply with any unconstitutional or illegal order from anyone if he does not order them to do so.

He reiterated that KP’s people and administration had made “countless sacrifices” in the fight against terrorism.

“If someone pushes you to follow any unconstitutional order, do not follow it. It can damage our province or the country.”

He also called on the chief secretary to urge the provincial administration not to indulge in any unconstitutional activity and to take action against those who were accused of corrupt practices.

The chief minister then took aim at Kundi’s PPP, blaming ex-president Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, along with General Yahya Khan, for the separation of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.

He accused President Asif Ali Zardari of “intending to make another East Pakistan here“.

“We will not allow any conspiracy to break up Pakistan to succeed,” he asserted.

“The party that raised the slogan of democracy separated Bangladesh from Pakistan in the past for its personal interests,” he alleged.

“Prioritising personal interests over national interests has been the PPP’s practice,” he further claimed.

Responding to Afridi, Kundi said on Geo News’ programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ said he called the meeting in light keeping in view the prevalent terrorism in the province.

He then went on accusing the PTI of facilitating and supporting terrorism.

The remarks by the CM and the governor come amid heightened tensions between the Centre and the PTI-led opposition, with the latter going ahead with its long march despite warnings from the Centre of action against any such move.

Hours-long talks over the weekend between a joint delegation of the government and PPP, and the opposition alliance ended in a deadlock, with both sides blaming the other for the breakdown.

Political temperatures have also remained high due to speculations of the Centre imposing governor’s rule in the province, with Kundi and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi discussing the move on Sunday.

‘Policy shift is necessary’

The KP CM also reiterated his objection to the Centre’s counterterrorism policy and defended his government’s efforts in supporting the police in the fight against terrorism.

He contended that terrorism had been “imposed on the province again”, asserting that the PTI-led provincial government had always supported the police and the people of KP.

Afridi maintained that he had been making efforts to strengthen the police, the Counter-Terrorism Department and Special Branch since he took the oath on Oct 15, 2025.

“The KP police have the most modern weapons and equipment compared with any other police force in Pakistan,” the chief minister said.

He contended that the federal government had always treated KP like a “stepchild”.

“The tribal districts were merged into KP in 2018, but they have not been fully integrated financially to this day,” CM Afridi claimed, adding that the financial rights of the tribal districts agreed upon at the time of their merger had not been provided yet.

The PTI leader went on to claim that federal governments had “continuously imposed military operations” on KP since 2004.

“People displaced by the federal government’s wrong policies kept crying on the streets, but they have still not received full compensation,” he said, adding that nearly Rs100 billion in compensation were still outstanding.

“Those whose homes were destroyed, families affected and mosques demolished are still wandering from pillar to post for their compensation.”

He highlighted that while a compensation of only Rs400,000 per household had been fixed for tribal families, they had not even been paid the promised amount.

Afridi stressed that a commitment was also made to provide between Rs370million and Rs380m per month to displaced people from North Waziristan at the Baka Khel camp. “The displaced people of Baka Khel are still not being provided the monthly amount as promised.”

“It is the provincial government’s responsibility to stand with people displaced by the federal government’s wrong policies,” the chief minister stated, adding that his government had provided Rs21bn for displaced people.

“The provincial government also has to bear responsibility for losses caused by military operations and collateral damage as a result of drone attacks,” Afridi said.

He also remarked that the individuals making decisions in the federal government had no sense of the difficulties faced by the people as a result of those decisions.

“If the federal government is sincere with KP, it should upgrade the province’s NFC (National Finance Commission) share and pay its outstanding dues of around Rs125bn to the province that has sacrificed 80,000 precious lives,” he demanded.

Afridi reaffirmed that KP had to fight terrorism as well as deal with the situation created by the federal government’s policies.

“The KP government and police are serious about maintaining law and order. Turning the police into personal servants and assigning them other tasks is wrong,” he declared.

“If the policy of KP’s stakeholders is followed, peace can be established within 100 days,” the PTI leader insisted.

He questioned why peace could not be established in the province “despite 14,000 intelligence-based operations and 22 major military operations over 22 years”, terming it a “failure of the federal policy”.

Afridi maintained that if the issue of peace still exists in KP even after 22 years, the federal government should change its policy against terrorism if it was “serious in doing so”.

“The excuse that KP is not cooperating is unacceptable; the same policy is also failing in Balochistan,” he claimed, as both provinces have witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years.

“The Balochistan government is cooperating with the federal government, but peace has still not been established there,” Afridi said, claiming the Centre’s counterterrorism policy was neither effective in KP nor in Balochistan.

“A shift in policy is necessary. KP can establish peace within 100 days,” he reaffirmed.

In his address, Afridi also once again criticised Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s remarks that her province faced no threats from India, despite the state’s narrative of the presence of Indian proxies in Pakistan in the face of Fitna al Hindustan.

Asif says ‘enough is enough’

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif assailed the PTI-led KP government for continuing its “complete detachment from terrorism in the province and criminal indifference”.

“Enough is enough!!!” he wrote in a post on X.

“The PTI provincial government is roaming the streets for a so-called failed political long march, while its facilitators have unleashed a fresh wave of terrorism against the people of KP during this very time,” he said.

The minister recalled Tuesday’s attacks in Dera Ismail Khan, where customs officials were among five people killed.

He remarked that the entire provincial cabinet, including the chief minister, was “numb to this serious matter and fully engrossed in their politically failed long march”.

“As always, these insensitive and shameless people did not even condemn the innocent murder of these five individuals in DI Khan, offered no condolences to the grieving families, did not attend their funerals or, at the very least, visit their homes to express regret,” Asif regretted.

“This is inexcusable by any standard.”

Instead, the defence minister noted, the KP CM had scheduled a meeting today at his party’s behest to reprimand the IG and chief secretary for attending the governor’s security meeting.

“The chief minister and his cabinet of a province under the scourge of terrorism have completely abandoned the province’s people to the mercy of the terrorists. That is why the people of KP are protesting against the provincial government on the streets in various areas.

“This can no longer be tolerated,” Asif declared.

The defence minister accused the KP government of being in “complete collusion” with terrorists, saying there was evidence available of “its facilitator ecosystem, which every Pakistani has witnessed with their own eyes over the past three years”.

Recalling past arrests of ex-premier Nawaz Sharif and his family members, as well as PML-N leaders, Asif asserted: “Time has proven that the allegations were just allegations and they were imprisoned on Imran Khan’s behest.”

Yet, he stressed, the PML-N fulfilled its parliamentary role responsibly under the Constitution and did not hold the country and institutions “hostage”.

“It fought a legal and constitutional battle in the courts and parliament. It did not ally with the Taliban,” Asif declared.

The defence minister said that the “time has come to make crucial decisions”.

“KP cannot be left any longer to the mercy of incompetent, insensitive rulers and Taliban allies,” he avowed.

Asif further stressed that the unity of the country cannot be put at risk. “An entire province cannot be held hostage. Enough is enough.”

item.title: Australia prepare for first test in South Africa since'Sandpapergate'
item.description:
Australia play their first test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal when they start a three-match series in Durban on Friday, with the visitors unlikely to face more than a few heckles over the incident that rocked the sport eight years ago.

The tourists efforts to roughen up the ball using sandpaper, and aid reverse swing, in Cape Town in March 2018 were caught on camera and led to a major reckoning for the game in Australia, with captain Steve Smith among those banned for their role in the subterfuge.

South Africa have played tests in Australia since Sandpapergate, and Australia have toured South Africa in the interim for limited-overs internationals.

The scandal has attracted little media focus in South Africa over recent weeks in comparison to the attention devoted to the incident in the Australian press.

After dethroning Australia last year in a thrilling World Test Championship final at Lords to win a first major title, South Africa are focused on improving their chances of a return to the final at the end of the 202527 WTC cycle.

Australia are also in need of a boost after a surprise home test defeat by Bangladesh in August and with an Ashes tour to England starting next June.

The pitch at Kingsmead often proves a fickle track but should offer the spinners a chance to play a leading role in a change from South Africas usually seamer-friendly surfaces.

It is unusual for South Africas chances to be largely entrusted to their spin attack, but Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj wreaked havoc in India last November when they triumphed in their last two test outings.

Spin was also a key factor for the home side as they beat Australia in the recent One-Day International series.

South Africa may therefore opt to rest frontline attack bowler Kagiso Rabada from the test as he continues his comeback from a hamstring injury.

Injury to Australia all-rounder Cameron Green opens up a chance at number five for Cooper Connolly, or a fairytale return for 34-year-old Nic Maddinson after recovering from cancer.

South Africas also has a choice to make over their number three batsman, with coach Shukri Conrad having several options including a potential first cap for 30-year-old Marques Ackerman.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis say struck Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
item.description:
SAUDI-YEMEN-IRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

Iran-backed Houthis said Monday they had struck Riyadh’s international airport, an oil refinery and other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.

Pakistan and Turkey have pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.

The fighting in Yemen has become the most active front in the Middle East war in recent weeks, displacing more than 184,000 people, the United Nations says, and deepening the conflict that has engulfed the wider region.

The Houthis previously controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the western city of Hodeida, but seized swathes of coastline last month along the Red Sea and key Bab al-Mandab Strait, in Yemen’s deadliest fighting in years.

The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.

The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.

Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit “military targets” belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.

They “destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines” and had “thwarted a planned attack” targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.

Later, the military said it had driven the Houthis from the area surrounding the Bab al-Mandeb Strait—a vital route for maritime traffic—including the port city of Mocha, Dhubab airport and Al-Omari military camp.

They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the southwest, where deadly fighting has surged in recent days.

Military sources stopped short of confirming an official announcement of Mocha’s recapture, saying that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the port.

UN ‘deeply concerned’

Loud explosions rattled the Saudi capital on Monday evening, with a Houthi spokesman saying the group had hit King Khalid International Airport, a refinery belonging to state oil giant Aramco and other targets in the kingdom’s south.

It came a day after Yemen’s government announced the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory—home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

Representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event of any attack.

They also agreed “to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.

The statement did not specify what role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.

A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”, and condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia.

Houthi attacks have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.

A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom’s exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.

Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war before the Houthis began targeting the world’s largest oil exporter.

Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were “scarily thin” owing to the war.

“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.

item.title: Bangladesh to buy 10 aircraft from Airbus, deal tomorrow
item.description:
After Boeing, the government is now set to purchase 10 aircraft from European aircraft manufacturer Airbus. A deal between state-owned Biman Bangladesh Airlines and Airbus will be signed tomorrow, Wednesday.

According to a statement issued by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the signing ceremony, titled 'Spreading Our Wings Together,' will be held at a hotel in the capital. Neither Bangladesh nor Airbus has yet disclosed how much the 10 aircraft will cost.

Under the proposed agreement, Biman will purchase four A350-900s and six A321neos from Airbus. The wide-body A350-900s will primarily be used on long-haul international routes, while the narrow-body A321neos will be deployed on regional and medium-haul routes.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism said Airbus could begin delivering the aircraft in 2033. The aircraft could be added to Biman’s fleet in phases through 2036 or 2037.

25 more aircraft to come from Boeing

Before signing the deal with Airbus, Biman signed two separate agreements this year to purchase a total of 25 aircraft from US aircraft manufacturer Boeing.

In the first deal, signed on 30 April, Biman agreed to purchase 14 aircraft for about USD 3.7 billion (approximately Tk 454 billion). The order includes eight 787-10 Dreamliners, two 787-9s and four 737-8s.

In the second deal, signed in New York on 23 September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Biman agreed to purchase another 11 aircraft. These include five 787-10s and six 737-8 MAX aircraft.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism said deliveries of the Boeing aircraft could begin in 2031. It will take 11 to 12 years to receive all the aircraft.

The ministry said Biman will not have to make payments immediately after the agreements are signed. Payment will be made when each aircraft is delivered. However, Biman authorities have requested that at least one aircraft be delivered in 2027 or 2028.

Biman’s current fleet

Biman currently has 19 aircraft in its fleet, including 14 Boeing aircraft and five Dash 8s.

However, two aircraft in the fleet are close to becoming unserviceable. The remaining 17 are also expected to be phased out within the next few years. To meet immediate demand, Biman is therefore trying to lease 10 more aircraft. Despite several attempts, the state-owned airline has yet to lease any aircraft.

Once Airbus’ 10 aircraft and the 25 Boeing aircraft under contract are added, Biman will have 35 new aircraft in the coming years. Including its current 19 aircraft, the airline’s fleet will exceed 50 aircraft.

According to Biman, of the 35 new aircraft, 19 will be wide-body aircraft and 16 will be narrow-body aircraft.

Most of Biman’s current fleet is made up of aircraft manufactured by US-based Boeing. With the addition of Airbus aircraft, Biman Bangladesh Airlines will, for the first time, operate a fleet comprising aircraft from both US and European manufacturers.

Paramount officially merges with Warner Bros. Here’s how we got here
item.description:
It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

The companies completed the deal on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood giant with the now shorter “Skydance” nametag. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together. And HBO Max, titles ranging from Harry Potter to Sinners, and even networks like CNN find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS, and the likes of Top Gun and The Godfather.

All of them will come under the helm of billionaire David Ellison and his new co-CEO, Ynon Kreiz. That further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. Ellison’s Skydance bought out Paramount for $8 billion just last year, and set its sights on Warner—an even bigger fish—very soon after.

What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight over Warner’s fate.

Skydance Corp. emerges from one of the biggest tie-ups ever in the media and entertainment industry. Including billions of dollars in debt, the Warner acquisition amounted to nearly $111 billion.

“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement Tuesday. “We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.”

Here’s a look at some of the key moments that got us here.

Netflix v. Paramount

The early days of Paramount’s quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war.

Months after disclosing it was open to selling parts or even all of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix back in December. But Skydance-owned Paramount, which claimed Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with its previous proposals, soon launched a hostile counterbid aimed at taking over the entire company—including networks like CNN and Discovery.

The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer on the table, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share, and Netflix opted to bow out of the race. Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement by late February.

The response from Hollywood

Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner’s future. And from awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known.

In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors, and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. The open letter—which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams—warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.”

Meanwhile, some other stars lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon this past spring, the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise—who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower with the words “the future is Paramount, and the future looks pretty great from here.” Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison.

The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season this year, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, Remarkably Bright Creatures actor Sally Field—who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal—stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.”

Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix’s studio and streaming deal was on the table, with particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters.

Trump and CNN

Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration wasn’t afraid to chime in about hopes for a new owner.

In December—days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner—the president said that CNN spreads “poison and lies,” adding that “I think the people who have run CNN for the last long period of time are a disgrace” and “it’s imperative that CNN be sold.”

The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network’s coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. At the time, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”

Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN, and under a since-finalized settlement with the states, the company also agreed to form a “News Editorial Independence Board.” But critics point to turmoil already seen at CBS under Skydance ownership—and aren’t convinced this new body will move the needle much, because Ellison is set to have ample oversight over appointments. Outside this board, however, the combined company is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN’s editor-in-chief.

Trump has separately continued to criticize CBS coverage under Skydance ownership. Still, the president has held a long relationship with the billionaire Ellison family. Paramount’s chief reportedly hosted a dinner in Washington in Trump’s honor back in April, on the same day Warner shareholders gave their greenlight for the merger. And in June, just two days after the U.S. Justice Department said it wouldn’t intervene in the deal, Ellison attended an Ultimate Fighting Championship match on the White House lawn for Trump’s 80th birthday (streamed by Paramount+).

Gulf money

To help fund its Warner buyout, Paramount racked up billions of dollars in financial backing from three Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request for sizeable indirect ownership from those foreign investors.

Paramount previously disclosed it expected those funds to indirectly own nearly 50% of equity interests—but no voting rights—of what is now the larger Skydance. But the company asked for clearance of up to 100% to account for potential future investments, which the FCC granted, citing in part that access to more capital would strengthen the broadcast industry and was therefore “in the public interest.”

Critics—including FCC’s sole Democratic Commissioner, Anna Gomez—have called the move alarming and unprecedented. They argue that amount of money opens the door to behind-the-scenes influence.

The final antitrust fight

Paramount cleared antitrust hurdles for its Warner acquisition from regulators worldwide over the summer, including the Trump administration’s Justice Department.

But in July, Democratic attorneys general from 12 states—led by California’s Rob Bonta—sued to block the merger, alleging the combined company would “extinguish competition” and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatergoers and cable customers across the U.S.

The Writers Guild of America followed suit. And Paramount agreed to put its Warner buyout on ice well into next year so the challenges could head toward a larger antitrust trial.

Settlement agreements emerged in September. The states’ terms, eventually approved by a judge, include pledges from the company to increase film production in the U.S. over the next five years, commit millions of dollars to a fund aimed at supporting workers displaced by the merger, and again establish new editorial monitoring of CNN and CBS.

Settling these challenges marked a key hurdle ahead of closing the deal. Critics decried the deal as capitulating to corporate pressure and said the remedies were too weak.

—By Wyatte Grantham-Philips, AP Business Writer

item.title: US risks ceding AI governance leadership to China and the EU
How America Wins the AI Race With Open Source
item.description:
Speaking in Shanghai on July 17, Xi Jinping offered the world a vision of AI “for the positive, for good and for humanity.” He called for open source, openness, and sharing. He cautioned against stretching national security to cover the field. And he announced that over the next five years China will train 5,000 people from developing countries, build AI application cooperation centers with ASEAN, the Arab League, the African Union, CELAC, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and BRICS, and extend its MAZU meteorological warning system to 30 countries. The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization now exists in Shanghai with 37 member states.

This reasonable sounding offer is aimed squarely at the governments the United States most needs: countries that want AI capacity, local control, and a voice in setting the rules. For these governments sovereignty means control rather than independence, and a system they can operate locally is an easier sell than a remotely controlled API. Beijing pairs capable open weight models and inexpensive inference with training, institutions, and public goods, then wraps the package in the vocabulary of multilateralism and the United Nations.

The results are already visible. CNAS counted sovereign AI initiatives in 67 countries and the European Union by mid-2026, up from 16 governments in 2023, and most model projects with disclosed foundations adapt a foreign open weight model rather than train one. Increasingly that foundation is Chinese. Spain’s Quasar 438B, billed as Europe’s strongest reasoning model, is built on Z.ai’s GLM-5.2. Japan’s Rakuten AI 3.0 uses the DeepSeek-V3 architecture. AI Singapore built its latest regional model on Alibaba’s Qwen rather than Meta’s Llama, and Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN commissioned its Arabic model from MiniMax. Chinese open-weight models passed the American share of global downloads for the first time in 2025, and on OpenRouter, a marketplace that routes developer traffic to models, their share of usage climbed from under 15 percent to more than half within a year, with businesses in the Global South the heaviest users.

The United States can win this competition, but not just by publishing the most advanced models and declaring victory. It must make American technology the preferred foundation for other countries’ AI systems, as American software and protocols became the foundation of the modern internet. That requires capable models, affordable hardware, financing, training, and dependable support, assembled into an offer that can stand beside a cheaper Chinese full-stack bid.

What America Must Do to Win

Washington should compete throughout hardware, models, software, and services. Retreating to frontier models and advanced chips while China supplies the open models, inexpensive inference, and industrial applications through which most of the world will actually use AI would surrender the contest at the layers where adoption happens.

Openness alone wins nothing. It gives a country seeking local control a reason to consider a model, not a reason to prefer an American one over a Chinese one. The American model must win on performance, total cost, local-language capability, reliable supply, and support, and it must leave room for domestic firms to build businesses around it. Partners deserve honest terms about licenses, updates, and what happens when a supplier relationship ends, and they have reason to ask. When U.S. controls forced Anthropic to suspend access to its newest models from June 12 to June 30, governments learned that even allies can lose access to American systems on a decision made in Washington. Autonomy has to be part of the product, because autonomy is what Beijing is selling.

The model is not hypothetical. An Indian financial firm runs DeepSeek on rented GPUs in India; the weights reside locally, inference never leaves the country, and there is no API for a foreign developer to revoke. Partners want the same from America, with the hardware, financing, and support that make it work. The developers now building on Qwen and DeepSeek show the cost of ceding that ground: expertise accumulates around particular models, models are tuned for particular hardware, and both pull future purchasing with them.

What China Is Doing

Xi’s language of openness should be read alongside that of Chen Yixin, China’s Minister of State Security. Writing in the Cyberspace Administration’s magazine in September, Chen describes AI as a primary battleground of great-power competition. He links political security, espionage, cyber capability, and military transformation to technological independence and control over international governance. An intelligence chief is explaining how AI alters the conditions under which his state exercises power. The two speeches are not in tension. One describes the offer; the other describes the objective.

The institutions Xi announced serve both. A cooperation center with each major regional bloc is a venue where Chinese models, hardware, and standards become the default for an entire region’s developers. A meteorological warning system deployed in 30 countries is a public good that also installs Chinese infrastructure and data flows in 30 capitals; an Egypt-specific version with aviation weather and sandstorm warnings is already in development, while Huawei courts Cairo for its Ascend chips and Malaysia weighs the same hardware. This is the softer sell: adapt the technology to the customer’s existing systems rather than demand reorganization around the supplier, as 01.AI did in building Kazakhstan’s national model. The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization is a bid to set governance terms in a body Beijing convened, and Xi’s warning against an expansive national security concept is a preemptive argument against the export controls Washington relies on. Washington should engage on international standards, but only where the decision rules leave Beijing no approval power over American development or release, at home or abroad.

Beijing’s openness may not last. Reuters reported in July that Chinese authorities were weighing restrictions on their own frontier models, and the TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released September 14 under CAC guidance, points the same way. Alongside provisions on loss of control and autonomous cyberattacks, its treatment of capability diffusion and removable safeguards suggests China may grow more selective about open releases. If so, its position as the default supplier of capable open models may not endure, and the window for an American alternative is open now.

The Tradeoff America Should Accept

Open models cannot be recalled once distributed. That is their appeal to partners, and it means adversaries will use them. The presumption should nonetheless favor open release. Any exception should identify the capability at issue, the security benefit of withholding it, the cost to American adoption, and whether adversaries can obtain comparable capability elsewhere. With a near-peer challenger offering alternatives, withholding American models may merely divert adoption without diminishing adversary capability. Washington can still restrict advanced chip exports for defined security reasons; a partner’s choice of competing hardware is a reason to improve the offer, not to penalize the partner.

Partner autonomy does not require surrendering American authority over domestic release decisions, export licensing, or the integrity of U.S. networks. It requires accepting that American benefits need not depend on a remote veto over systems partners already operate. Government and military users at home should continue to choose systems, closed or open, on performance and security.

What Washington Should Do

The July 2025 AI Action Plan endorses open-source and open-weight AI, and Executive Order 14320 on exporting the American AI stack supplies a framework for coordinated technology packages, diplomacy, and financing. The task is to convert those commitments into an offer that wins.

Fund what the market will undersupply: sustained open releases, smaller-language capability, independent evaluation, and affordable local deployment. Make the complete package competitive, with financing, predictable hardware access, workforce training, and genuine roles for local firms, and resource it as the national security priority it is. The Export-Import Bank’s $66.1 million guarantee for Côte d’Ivoire’s national data center shows the tools exist; it needs to operate at the scale of China’s regional cooperation centers. Demonstrate the bargain with willing partners through a sovereign AI pilot, potentially building on Pax Silica, that discloses remaining dependencies and compares cost, delivery time, and power requirements against the alternatives. Each regional cooperation center Beijing opens should have an American counterpart that partners can judge on results. Then measure the results: which models partners choose, whose hardware serves them, and who earns the integration revenue. A lost American sale does not always deepen dependence on China, and a won one does not always reduce it.

American leadership will prove most durable when partners have their own reasons to sustain it. The test is what countries choose to build, and whether building with America remains worth it to them.

item.title: Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness
item.description:
Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness Expert comment jon.wallace 7 October 2026

Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric should be taken seriously. But Baltic states know grey zone attacks and territorial incursions are equally serious threats.

Vladimir Putin always chooses his words carefully. If Russia faced a direct attack on Kaliningrad (its enclave on the Baltic Sea), he warned on 1 October, the use of ‘all weapons in (our) country’s arsenal’ would inevitably be on the table. 

The statement followed an earlier Russian note to NATO, threatening nuclear escalation if the alliance were to isolate Kaliningrad. NATO, thus far, has responded with restraint. Secretary General Mark Rutte said there was no imminent Russian threat and rebuffed Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric. But this skirmishing has pushed Kaliningrad – and NATO’s Baltic borders with Russia – back into the spotlight. 

Kaliningrad is not just any territory for the Russians. At the Yalta and Potsdam conferences of 1945, Soviet leader Stalin asserted his claim to what was then known as Königsberg. It was, he said, necessary for Russia to have at least ‘one ice-free port’ at the expense of Germany. The US and UK consented, and Moscow gained a permanent military position on the Baltic Sea. 

After the collapse of the Soviet Union and the withdrawal of the Baltic states to become independent democracies, Kaliningrad’s geographical isolation from Russia became more apparent, creating one of the most peculiar pieces of land on the continent. Today the enclave hosts Russia’s Baltic Fleet, missile systems and combat aircraft. 

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the surrounding geopolitics has changed. Finland and Sweden are now part of NATO. Poland is rearming at unprecedented speed. And the military presence across the alliance’s north-eastern flank is much denser. Meanwhile, Lithuania may soon vote to lift a ban on hosting nuclear weapons on its territory – a move the Kremlin described on 6 October as ‘a step towards escalating tensions’.

Kaliningrad remains a key forward position for Russia. But its near-complete isolation, in the middle of a more coherent NATO Baltic presence, presents Moscow with a serious geostrategic and military challenge.

Denying Russia a quick victory

One glance at the map is enough to understand that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have but little strategic depth. The three states depend heavily on the Suwałki corridor – a 65km strip of land between Kaliningrad and Belarus that connects Poland and Lithuania – for overland reinforcement. Reclaiming territory from an attacker would be an unlikely option for Baltic countries.

The only credible alternative is to make a Russian advance difficult from the beginning. ‘We have to start from the border and win from the first battles,’ Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the Estonian First Brigade, recently declared.

That is the purpose of the Baltic Defence Line along the eastern border: bunkers, anti-tank obstacles and other defensive outposts. Estonia plans hundreds of squad-level bunkers. A permanently deployed German armoured brigade will become operational in Lithuania in 2027. And Finland now hosts a NATO Forward Land Force. Defence spending across the region has risen far beyond NATO’s old two-per-cent target to reach nearly 5.5 per cent in the case of Estonia.

The intention is clear. Russia must be deterred from any attempt to seize even a small amount of territory – a significant possibility if Russia were to test NATO resolve. 

Preparedness before the first bullet is shot

But Baltic defence measures are about more than spending commitments and defending their Russian borders. Baltics countries know that to deter Russia it is just as vital to stress test their critical infrastructure and train their societies to keep functioning if and when a crisis emerges. Indeed, there is a lot the rest of the continent could learn from Baltic states’ whole-of-society model, which seeks to prepare their entire populations for an era of high-threat risk. 

From Finland to Lithuania, this model consists of embedding all the layers of society in defence and preparedness strategies. This form of ‘comprehensive security’ is grounded in the belief that keeping the country functioning in a crisis is a shared responsibility of government, business, civil society and citizens. In this regard, the Baltics are the most strategically advanced in Europe.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have accelerated preparations for grey zone conflict of the kind in which Russia excels, including attacks on infrastructure. All three have disconnected their electricity systems from Russian and Belarusian networks, progressively synchronizing them with the continental grid since February 2025. In the meantime, NATO has increased protection of Baltic undersea infrastructure, following damaged cables and various incidences of suspected sabotage. 

Slowly learning

Europe’s larger military powers are awaking to the need to somehow follow the Baltic lead and prepare their societies for an enlarging spectrum of threats. Germany, which would serve as one of NATO’s main logistical hubs in any reinforcement of the Baltic region, saw much of its civil-defence architecture fall into disrepair after the fall of the Berlin Wall. 

Its shelter capacity, for instance, now covers only around 480,000 people. Last spring Berlin approved a new €10-billion civil-defence programme, including plans to convert underground car parks, tunnels and stations into emergency shelters – evidence of renewed political engagement.

France has tested its armed forces at scale in the Orion 26 high-intensity exercise, which brought together 12,500 troops, 24 allied nations and civilian institutions in a scenario ranging from hybrid attacks to large-scale conventional war. The UK has developed a 2026 resilience plan that explicitly acknowledges growing Russian sub-threshold attacks. And the government is considering a reserve-style home-defence force to protect critical infrastructure. 

These are important changes. But ‘E3’ countries are still struggling to jointly improve resilience in transport, healthcare, energy, and communications – even as the risk of an enemy trying to disrupt all of them at once grows.

NATO is moving to drive the task forward. Its newly released resilience baseline requirements ask governments to plan for large movements of populations alongside military deployments; to develop health systems that can function even in case of mass casualties; and to develop communications and transport networks that can continue supporting allied forces during high-intensity conflict. In the near future, these will become the pillars on which deterrence actually depends.

Baltic gaps

Still, resilience won’t be enough alone to vanquish an enemy attack on the region. Baltic air and missile defence remains rather thin considering the scale of Russia’s drone and missile arsenal. Reinforcements would still have to reach the region through corridors like the Suwałki gap. And Russia would seize any opportunity to disrupt such movements. Fundamentally, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania remain reliant on their larger allies’ ability to swiftly provide additional forces and air power in the event of a significant attack.

This makes Stalin’s ‘ice-free port’ of Kaliningrad more than an isolated flashpoint on the Baltic shores. Putin’s nuclear rhetoric deserves to be taken seriously. Russia revised its nuclear doctrine in 2024, explicitly broadening the circumstances in which Moscow could consider nuclear use. These include threats to its territorial integrity and attempts to isolate parts of the Russian territory. 

But the military geography surrounding the enclave has changed too. Once referred to as NATO’s most exposed flank, the Baltics have become much harder to intimidate, and harder still to overrun before NATO can respond. 

Related work

Poland could be Europe’s rising star on defence and security

Their experience also carries a wider lesson for Europe: strategic weight is not measured by size alone, even that of a nuclear arsenal. Agility, civil preparedness and political resolve have allowed small states, free and democratic since 1991, to alter the terms of deterrence at their border. 

They have shown Europe that resilience begins long before deterrence fails and that it can change the enemy’s calculation. Their measures will make any attack look potentially far slower and costlier that Moscow would once have believed. Perhaps most significantly after the blatant failure of Russian objectives in Ukraine, Baltic resilience makes overall success of a military attack look far less certain for Vladimir Putin.

item.title: After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces
item.description:
After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces Expert comment thilton.drupal 7 October 2026

The threat of hybrid attacks from Iran and Russia means the UK should develop a force dedicated to protecting its bases and infrastructure at home. Finland and Poland offer lessons.

The US’s withdrawal of its bombers from RAF Fairford, following a suspected terror plot against the base, has brought attention to how the UK defends its homeland military bases and other critical infrastructure.

The UK government has insisted RAF Fairford is safe following the arrest of five men near the base on 27 September. President Donald Trump said the US withdrew its bombers from the base because of an unspecified ‘threat’ to the base. 

The investigation into the incident is still ongoing. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that there are ‘strong indications that Iran played a part,’ which Iran’s embassy in London has rejected. In March, the UK approved a US request to use RAF Fairford for what it described as defensive strikes on Iran. Tehran responded that any base used for ‘aggression against Iranian territory’ would be a ‘legitimate target’ for its forces.

Bases such as Fairford have their own protection forces that guard the perimeter. But incidents like this highlight the need for the UK to improve its wider homeland defence forces in the face of sustained pressure from hostile actors such as Iran and Russia. 

While the UK has specialist counter-terrorism units that can respond to incidents, and its armed forces and reserves can be deployed domestically to aid civil authorities in a crisis, it lacks a specialist domestic-only force that could protect a wider range of sites for a longer period.

Response versus protection 

The Fairford incident is just one example of the various hybrid threats facing the UK. Alongside Iran, Russia in particular poses a major threat. The Cabinet Office recently announced it would brief the chief executives of UK critical national infrastructure providers and defence firms on the ‘enduring and significant threat’ from Russia. 

Danish intelligence has also warned that Russia could mount a limited military attack against a NATO member within months. Across Europe, states have attributed drone incursions, arson and sabotage to Russia.

Protecting domestic sites is different to identifying the perpetrators or deciding on retaliatory measures. These happen after an attack; protection must be in place before one. This requires forces built for protection, not just response – which is what some UK allies already have. 

Poland and Finland’s approaches

Poland and Finland have both taken a structural approach, creating forces whose primary purpose is the defence of their own territory. 

Established in 2017, Poland’s Territorial Defence Force is the fifth branch of its armed forces. Recruited locally and organized around a brigade in each province, it remains in its own province when Poland mobilizes its forces, rather than reinforcing the regular military. Its stated tasks include protecting critical national infrastructure. 

Related work

Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness

Finland’s approach is broader. A permanent security committee coordinates preparedness across government, working from a list of key functions that the state must keep running in a crisis such as water, energy and transport. Military and civilian planning sits within a single framework rather than separate departments. The premise is that defending the home territory is a permanent task, rather than a contingency to be activated during a conflict.  

Neither of these two models directly transfers to the UK. Poland’s territorial force reflects its position bordering Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad. Finland’s rests on conscription and a political culture influenced by its long border with Russia. 

However, the principle beneath both examples is transferable: protecting home territory requires forces raised specifically for the task, not carved out of regular forces each time they are needed. 

The UK has currently not adopted this principle. It does not have a dedicated force assigned to protecting a wide set of UK sites for a long period. 

Architecture without dedicated forces 

The UK is not starting from scratch. 

The Cabinet Office runs the Home Defence Programme, a cross-government effort to align military and civilian planning for threats to the UK. The 2026 Resilience Action Plan implementation report said the programme was being accelerated, with updated crisis response protocols and a planned national home defence exercise in 2027. The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has a Director of Homeland Defence and Strategic Threats. Standing Joint Command is the MOD’s operational headquarters for UK resilience tasks. 

A report published in January by researchers at the University of Exeter set out what this architecture lacks. The report argues that home defence activity is fragmented; that no lead department holds a mandate with executive tasking authority and adequate resources; and that the UK is at a standing start while allies including Finland, Poland and the Baltic states are years ahead. Its recommendation of a designated lead department is a good starting point.

However, even if these recommendations were implemented, a mandate does not produce troops. The UK has a reserve force. But alongside maintaining the UK’s own defence and resilience, this force is also expected to contribute to NATO’s collective defence and can be deployed abroad. 

Relying on the same reservists for both tasks only works while these two demands do not arrive at the same time. UK land forces are designed on the assumption that they will be deployed abroad, rather than defend domestic sites. In a crisis on the European continent, the task of domestic protection would not disappear. It would compete with the demand for British land forces to be deployed elsewhere.

Three changes the UK should make

Three changes follow. The UK should base its approach on the Polish design principle. This means setting up new reserve sub-units with a purely domestic protective role, recruited and based locally. These new units would be positioned near the bases and critical national infrastructure most likely to attract attention, and not counted as reinforcements for deploying formations elsewhere.

The new units would not replace existing forces. Guard forces such as the MOD Police and the Military Provost Guard Service, along with the RAF Regiment for air bases, would remain responsible for perimeters and immediate site security. And specialist units would still respond to incidents. 

Instead, the new units would do what the existing forces are not designed to do: secure non-military critical infrastructure, cover the ground beyond the perimeters, and protect multiple locations during a period of heightened threat. They would be designed to hold these sites for periods of months rather than days. 

This does come at a cost. Every reservist given a home defence role is one fewer available for deployment, and that is a real reduction in what the UK can send abroad. But in a situation when both home defence and overseas demands occur, the choice of home defence will need to be prioritized by default. Making that choice deliberately now means the force is generated and ready before that happens. 

From Finland, the UK should take the treatment of homeland protection as a permanent function rather than a contingency. This means protecting a budget for it, since activity funded from training and readiness budgets is vulnerable when defence budgets are squeezed. The British Army has already reportedly been told to suspend major exercises this year for lack of funds, and in September it was reported that army reservists are set to serve fewer days because of budget cuts. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Finally, the UK’s distribution of its protective forces should follow from the government’s decisions and the threats those decisions potentially attract, rather than from isolated incidents. When the government permits an operation from British territory, as it did at Fairford, it should decide the protective requirements at the site and its surrounding areas at the same time. 

The UK has the intelligence capability and the legal framework to protect its domestic sites. It also has the beginnings of a coordinating structure, though it needs a clearer lead. What it now also needs is a dedicated force assigned to protecting those sites across the homeland.

item.title: The growing protests against India's poll body — and PM Modi
item.description:
India’s election commission is facing mounting pressure after a newspaper investigation alleged misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision.

The Indian Express alleged last month that key decisions linked to the large-scale revision exercise — which has seen millions of names removed from draft voter rolls — were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.

The Election Commission of India (ECI), a constitutional body, has rejected the allegations. It says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid.

Opposition parties say legitimate voters are being struck off to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.

Protests demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down have grown since the report, with a demonstration in the capital New Delhi on Saturday expected to draw large crowds.

The allegations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi, in his third term in office, following student protests in July that forced the education minister to resign.

Here is a rundown of the major issues at stake in the latest protest:

What’s the controversy?

The Indian Express reported that the poll body has been riven by internal disagreements since the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter lists began in 2025.

It said two of the ECI’s three commissioners formally lodged objections more than a dozen times in the last 10 months over key SIR decisions.

Decisions by the three-member poll body should be taken by consensus or a majority.

Why has it sparked anger?

The poll body says the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from casting ballots.

Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

How many are excluded?

According to election commission data cited by Indian media, more than 133 million names have been excluded from draft rolls.

That’s roughly the population of Mexico and, in the world’s most populous nation, adds up to about 15 per cent of the electorate.

The exclusions include duplicate entries and people found to have died.

The final count of excluded voters, however, will only be clear after claims and objections are processed and final rolls are published.

How big are the protests?

Thousands have taken to the streets in protest, and the youth-led online Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement launched fresh demonstrations on October 2 in Mumbai.

The opposition Congress Party has rallied in New Delhi, with key leader Rahul Gandhi briefly detained on both Tuesday and Wednesday.

The CJP, which has millions of followers on social media, succeeded in its campaign to oust the education minister in July over irregularities in exam systems.

The movement has called for another “mass mobilisation” on Saturday, supported by student groups aligned with left-wing parties.

“Last time when we got together, it was a cabinet minister who had to resign,” said Neha Bora, a student leader who has emerged as one of the faces of the latest protests.

“This time, we will see the CEC (chief election commissioner) being ousted.”

Who is Kumar?

Kumar, 62, is a retired civil servant from the elite Indian Administrative Service.

He took charge as election commission chief in February last year and is due to remain in office until January 2029.

Kumar’s civil services journey began in the southern state of Kerala, whose government launched a probe this month into corruption allegations involving him dating back to 2006.

What do the courts say?

The Supreme Court has ordered the government and election body to explain decisions linked to the voter-roll revision.

The legality of the revision exercise has also been examined by the court.

In May, it allowed the election commission to proceed with the nationwide exercise, while calling for safeguards to protect eligible voters.

Another hearing is due next week.

Seven years on, Abrar Fahad's family still waits for execution of verdict
item.description:
Seven years after the killing of Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) student Abrar Fahad, his elderly parents are still waiting to see the execution of the verdict in the case.
A Dhaka court in December 2021 sentenced 20 people to death and five others to life imprisonment in the sensational murder case that sparked huge outcry across the coutnry.
The High Court upheld the sentences on March 16, 2025.
However, the judicial process has not yet reached its final stage as appeals against the High Court verdict remain pending before the Appellate Division.
Abrar’s family said that although verdicts have been delivered at two levels of the judiciary, their wait for the case to reach its conclusion continues.
Abrar’s younger brother Abrar Faiyaz said the killing had a profound impact not only on their family but also on the country’s political and social landscape.
“Fascism’s exit began with Abrar Fahad’s murder. But the trial of those responsible for the killing that contributed to the change in Bangladesh’s political scenario is still unfinished,” he told over the phone.
He said his family contacted the relevant authorities after the High Court verdict in March 2025, but were told that cases are being dealt with according to their serial numbers.
“Cases can be taken up earlier in the serial. But they are hesitant to bring this case forward. We have contacted everyone we needed to. Now there is nothing left for us to do but wait,” he said.
“We do not know what is preventing the execution of the verdict. At this point, it feels like nothing but neglect,” Faiyaz said.
Abrar’s father, Md Barkat Ullah, also expressed frustration over the delay.
“Execution of the verdict against Abrar’s killers is not only my family’s demand; it is the demand of people across Bangladesh. Yet the sentences are not being carried out. I am not the only one disappointed by this — everyone in the country is,” he said over the phone.
“We still have not received complete justice. I appeal to the government to complete the judicial process as soon as possible,” he said.
Barkat Ullah said the family never imagined that their son, a student of one of the country’s premier educational institutions, would be brutally killed in such a manner.
National Citizens Party (NCP) Kushtia district member secretary Sultan Mahmud Talha said the authorities should take steps to execute the court verdict.
“The movement against fascism began with Abrar Fahad’s killing. That system has since been removed, and successive governments are benefiting from the circumstances created by his killing. They should ensure the execution of the sentences,” he said.
Abrar, a student of the Electrical and Electronic Engineering Department at BUET, was beaten to death at Sher-e-Bangla Hall on the night of Oct 6, 2019.
His father filed a murder case with Chawkbazar Police Station. After investigation, police submitted a charge sheet against 25 BUET students on Nov 13, 2019.
After more than two years of trial, a Dhaka court sentenced 20 accused to death and five to life imprisonment on Dec 8, 2021. The High Court later upheld the sentences after hearing the death references and appeals filed by the convicts.
The killing sparked widespread protests and public outrage and prompted renewed debate over student politics, political influence on campuses and violence in residential halls.

item.title: Pacific presses world for help ‘surviving’ climate change at pre-COP summit
item.description:
Pacific leaders pressed wealthy nations for more funds to help them “survive” climate change Wednesday at a gathering aimed at drawing the world’s attention to life on the frontline of global warming.
This week’s “pre-COP” meetings in the Fijian city of Nadi are a precursor to the larger UN-sponsored global climate summit -- known as COP31 -- to be held in Turkiye next month.
The South Pacific is among the regions of the world most vulnerable to global warming -- from rising seas jeopardizing homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
Speaking on the sidelines of the summit, Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape told journalists it was an issue of “morality.”
“Nations who have sovereign borders are facing the threat of being nations no more,” he said.
“We live with the burden of decisions made elsewhere.”
Pacific nations are using the pre-COP platform to push for more backing for the countries most affected by climate change.
The EU’s climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told journalists, “We’re clearly not doing enough.”
A UN report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion-$365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.
Regional leaders have set up the Pacific Resilience Facility with the hopes of raising $500 million, but it has so far brought in commitments for less than half of that.
Fiji on Wednesday announced an addition of $10 million for that fund.
The country’s climate minister Lynda Tabuya told AFP one of her main messages to delegates in Nadi was the need to speed up the distribution of money for climate solutions.
“Part of our appeal going to COP is to make the current finance structure to be restructured so that it’s simplified,” she said.
“It’s frustrating. We are the least emitters in the Pacific, and yet we are the most disproportionately affected.”
The Australian government also said it would invest AU$3 million in a number of regional road and communications infrastructure projects in Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Kiribati and Tuvalu.
Australia’s climate minister Chris Bowen said the money would “help these countries adjust to climate change, particularly focused on the coastlines with erosion, with rising sea levels.”
Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5°C.
Scientists agree that warming above 1.5°C relative to pre-industrial times poses grave risks, and nearly 200 nations committed a decade ago to try and keep global temperature rises to this safer threshold.
On Wednesday, AFP accompanied dozens of campaigners from the Pacific and Australia’s Torres Strait Islanders on a flotilla which sailed past the summit venue and urged leaders to “keep 1.5°C alive.”
Poiongo Lisati from Fiji’s Kioa Island said they hoped to “protect our people and also our land.”
“If climate finance assistance can be made available for the maritime islands, it will be easy for us to get help,” Lisati said.
On Tuesday, over a dozen leaders visited the nearby Pacific nation of Tuvalu, one of the world’s least-visited countries already laying plans to relocate its population of 10,600 if its islands are consumed by the ocean.
A marine heatwave in 2024 wiped out an estimated 99.9% of the coral that built the remote Tuvalu islands.
With just a few hours on the archipelago before flying back to Fiji, there was a rush from organizers to get in as many events as possible.
“The objective of this Tuvalu event is for you, leaders, to experience and feel climate change first-hand, from being in the frontline of the impact of climate change,” Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told visiting officials.

item.title: Thailand floods death toll rises to 60 since mid-September
item.description:
Flooding in Thailand since mid-September has killed 60 people nationwide, the government said on Wednesday, with river water levels still rising in some regions.
Days of heavy rain late last month inundated parts of the capital Bangkok, although the floods there have largely receded.
The situation remains difficult for many people in central Prachinburi province, where 19 people died, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation.
Overflowing rivers flooded houses in seven districts in the province, affecting more than 188,000 people, the department said in a statement.
People have died in around a dozen other provinces and the capital, with flooding ongoing in 27 of Thailand’s 77 provinces, it said.
In Bangkok, four people have died since September 16, after a month’s worth of rain fell over several days in late September, prompting a city-wide disaster declaration.
A massive clean-up is currently underway as the city prepares to host the IMF and World Bank meetings, which begin next week.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, whose government has faced public criticism over its flood response, ordered government agencies on Monday to manage flooding and transportation to avoid disruptions to the meetings.
September is the peak of Thailand’s rainy season, but this year felt worse for many in Bangkok, a city built on former marshlands and intersected by a network of canals.
Some areas were under knee-deep water for several days, with vehicles abandoned on submerged streets and schools closed for two days.

'Bangladesh Climate Development Partnership Knowledge Conference 2026' opens in Dhaka
item.description:
Over 500 global and national climate leaders, policymakers, development partners, private sector executives, and civil society representatives convened in Dhaka for the opening of the two-day Bangladesh Climate Development Partnership Knowledge Conference 2026, reports a press release.

Organised by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change with support of the Asian Development Bank, the landmark conference aims to accelerate the execution of the Bangladesh National Adaptation Plan 2023 to 2050 and the strategic investment frameworks of Nationally Determined Contributions 3.0.

A major highlight of the opening day was the official launch of the BCDP Web Portal alongside the Climate Solutions Exhibition.

This new digital platform serves as a centralised hub for real-time project tracking, pipeline management, data integration, and cross-sector coordination to streamline domestic and international climate investments.

The conference also reinforces the Bangladesh Climate Development Partnership, originally established in 2024, as the unified national institutional vehicle for climate finance mobilisation, resource allocation, and policy alignment.

Furthermore, upcoming sessions will center on scaling up investments in key sectors including energy transition, sustainable transport, water resource management, and climate-resilient agriculture.

Inaugurating the event, Abdul Awal Mintoo, member of parliament and honorable minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, officially unveiled the BCDP Web Portal and emphasised the long-term impact of current infrastructure and economic planning.

The Minister noted that today's development decisions will define the contours of climate risks for decades to come. He stressed that the primary task ahead is to translate national policies and frameworks into coordinated programmes, quality projects, appropriate financing, and measurable outcomes.

He highlighted the unique financial characteristics of adaptation initiatives, which yield essential social welfare benefits without standard commercial yields, and called for climate finance frameworks to align with Bangladesh's fiscal landscape.

He urged expanded private sector participation in clean energy, advocated for climate justice regarding Loss and Damage, and insisted on the inclusive participation of women, youth, persons with disabilities, and marginalised communities in project design and governance.

Delivering remarks on behalf of the Asian Development Bank, Satya Srinivas Lolla, executive director representing Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Lao PDR, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan, addressed the dual dynamics of Bangladesh's graduation from the Least Developed Country category and its ongoing climate vulnerabilities.

Satya Srinivas Lolla stated that the true success of this conference will be determined not by the discussions, but by the actions and investments that follow. Turning ambition into reality will require substantial investment from both the public and private sectors.

He explained that the core objective of the partnership is to bring together financing, technical expertise, institutional capacity, and partnerships, so that Bangladesh can move from ambition to implementation.

The inaugural session brought together distinguished leaders across the government and development sectors. Among the key participants were Sheikh Faridul Islam, honorable state minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Md Saimum Parvez, special assistant to the Prime Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and ABM Abdus Sattar, principal secretary to the Prime Minister's Office.

The welcome remarks were delivered by Mohammad Navid Shafullah, additional secretary for Climate Change at the Ministry, while the session was chaired by Fahmida Khanom, acting secretary of the Ministry.

The first day included three strategic plenary sessions. The first plenary, titled Pathways to Resilience and Low Carbon Growth, established macro strategic frameworks for navigating economic progress amidst escalating climate risks.

The second plenary focused on the practical implementation of the National Adaptation Plan 2023 to 2050, addressing localised implementation, sectoral cost modeling, and integration with national budget allocation processes. The third plenary evaluated Multilateral Development Bank financial instruments and mechanisms for blending public and private capital pipelines to implement Nationally Determined Contributions 3.0.

The conference concludes tomorrow, 8 October, 2026, with focused working groups and technical sessions dedicated to de-risking climate investments, building investment-ready project pipelines, and establishing public-private financing structures across energy, transport, and agricultural sectors.
